html:
The journey of the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta across the Sahara to the Mali Empire in 1352 and 1353, his last great trip. His account is one of the few eyewitness descriptions of Mali at its height.

He had already travelled for decades, as far as India, see Ibn Battuta reaches Delhi, and China. Sent by the sultan of Morocco, he crossed the desert with a camel caravan by way of Taghaza, a town whose houses were built of salt, to Walata, and then on to the capital of Mali, whose site is still unknown. He stayed about eight months at the court of Mansa Sulayman, the brother of Mansa Musa.

His report is mixed. He grumbled about the mansa's mean welcome gift, and he was shocked that women went about freely and some servant girls uncovered. But he praised the safety of the roads, the justice of the rulers and the people's care for prayer and learning the Quran. He returned by way of Timbuktu and Gao. Back in Morocco he dictated his travels, the Rihla, to a scribe. The trip shows the reach of the trans-Saharan trade that joined West Africa to the Mediterranean world.
sum: The journey of the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta across the Sahara to the Mali Empire in 1352 and 1353, his last great trip. His account is one of the few eyewitness descriptions of Mali at its height.
